questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The best initial screening test for Cushing's syndrome in an outpatient with central obesity and purple striae is:
questions.concept: Random cortisol is uninterpretable because of pulsatile secretion; the low-dose dexamethasone test, late-night salivary cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol are the three accepted screens, and ACTH is measured only after hypercortisolism is proved.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 379 (Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Hyperpigmentation of buccal mucosa and palmar creases in an adrenal insufficiency patient indicates:
options: Primary adrenal insufficiency with high ACTH
questions.concept: ACTH is cleaved from POMC, which also yields melanocyte-stimulating hormone; only primary (adrenal-level) failure raises ACTH enough to pigment the skin, so pituitary causes are pale.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 379 (Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest cause of primary hyperaldosteronism worldwide is:
questions.concept: Bilateral hyperplasia now outnumbers Conn's adenoma in screened hypertensive cohorts and matters because it is treated medically with spironolactone rather than by adrenalectomy.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 379 (Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A hypertensive patient has hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, and a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio. The next step is:
options: Confirmatory saline suppression or fludrocortisone test
questions.concept: The ratio only screens; aldosterone must be shown to be non-suppressible before imaging and adrenal vein sampling decide between adenoma and hyperplasia.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 379 (Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: In adrenal crisis the single most important immediate measure is:
questions.concept: Hydrocortisone 100 mg supplies both glucocorticoid and enough mineralocorticoid activity, and volume repletion corrects the hypovolaemic hypotension that vasopressors alone will not reverse.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 379 (Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An incidentally found 3 cm adrenal mass with Hounsfield unit value under 10 on unenhanced CT is most likely:
questions.concept: Attenuation below 10 HU reflects intracytoplasmic lipid, which is characteristic of a benign cortical adenoma; malignant and catecholamine-secreting lesions are lipid-poor and denser.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 379 (Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Persistent hypertension after biochemical cure of Cushing's syndrome is best explained by:
questions.concept: Long-standing cortisol excess produces structural arterial and renal change that does not reverse when cortisol normalises, so many patients need continued antihypertensive therapy.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 379 (Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with ACTH-dependent Cushing's fails to suppress on high-dose dexamethasone and has hypokalaemia with rapid onset of weakness. The most likely source is:
options: Ectopic ACTH from a small-cell lung carcinoma
questions.concept: Ectopic tumours lack glucocorticoid feedback receptors so they do not suppress at high dose, and their extreme cortisol levels overwhelm renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase to give a florid mineralocorticoid picture.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 379 (Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Hyponatraemia in Addison's disease is caused mainly by:
options: Aldosterone deficiency plus loss of cortisol restraint on vasopressin
questions.concept: Sodium is lost through mineralocorticoid deficiency while absent cortisol permits inappropriate vasopressin release, so free water is retained on top of the sodium loss.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 379 (Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The earliest laboratory abnormality in developing iron deficiency is:
questions.concept: Ferritin mirrors storage iron, which is exhausted before transport iron falls and long before erythropoiesis becomes iron-restricted enough to change cell size or haemoglobin.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 97 (Iron Deficiency and Other Hypoproliferative Anemias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A raised red cell distribution width with a normal MCV in an anaemic patient suggests:
options: Combined iron and vitamin B12 deficiency
questions.concept: Microcytes from iron deficiency and macrocytes from B12 deficiency average to a normal MCV, but the population is heterogeneous, which is exactly what a high RDW measures.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 97 (Iron Deficiency and Other Hypoproliferative Anemias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Oral iron is best absorbed when given:
options: On an empty stomach with vitamin C
questions.concept: Ferrous iron needs an acid environment and ascorbate keeps it reduced, whereas calcium, phytates, tannins and acid suppression all convert it to poorly absorbed ferric salts.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 97 (Iron Deficiency and Other Hypoproliferative Anemias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: In a patient with megaloblastic anaemia, hypersegmented neutrophils and a normal serum B12, the most useful next test is:
questions.concept: Serum B12 is insensitive in early deficiency; methylmalonic acid rises only in B12 deficiency while homocysteine rises in both B12 and folate deficiency, which separates the two.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 97 (Iron Deficiency and Other Hypoproliferative Anemias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Anaemia of chronic disease is distinguished from iron deficiency mainly by:
options: Normal or raised ferritin with low transferrin saturation
questions.concept: Hepcidin traps iron in macrophages, so stores are adequate or high while delivery to the marrow is poor, and hepcidin also lowers rather than raises the binding capacity.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 97 (Iron Deficiency and Other Hypoproliferative Anemias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Treating vitamin B12 deficiency with folate alone is dangerous because:
options: Haematological response occurs while neurological damage progresses
questions.concept: Folate bypasses the methionine synthase block for DNA synthesis but not for methylmalonyl-CoA metabolism, so subacute combined degeneration advances behind a correcting blood count.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 97 (Iron Deficiency and Other Hypoproliferative Anemias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A brisk reticulocytosis about one week after starting iron therapy indicates:
options: An appropriate marrow response confirming the diagnosis
questions.concept: The reticulocyte peak at day 5 to 10 is the earliest proof that the anaemia was iron-responsive, and haemoglobin should then rise by about 1 g/dL every two to three weeks.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 97 (Iron Deficiency and Other Hypoproliferative Anemias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Pancytopenia with a hypercellular marrow, raised LDH and low haptoglobin in a patient with nocturnal haemoglobinuria points to:
questions.concept: Loss of the GPI anchor removes CD55 and CD59 from red cells, exposing them to complement lysis; flow cytometry for those markers has replaced the older Ham and sucrose lysis tests.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 97 (Iron Deficiency and Other Hypoproliferative Anemias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An irregularly irregular pulse with absent P waves on the ECG indicates:
options: Second degree AV block Mobitz I
questions.concept: Chaotic atrial activity produces fibrillatory waves rather than P waves and variable AV conduction gives the irregular ventricular response.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 249 (The Tachyarrhythmias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The rate of atrial depolarisation in typical atrial flutter is approximately:
questions.concept: The macro-reentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus cycles at about 300, so a 2 to 1 block gives the classic ventricular rate near 150 with sawtooth waves in the inferior leads.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 249 (The Tachyarrhythmias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Progressive PR prolongation followed by a dropped beat describes:
options: Mobitz type I second degree AV block
questions.concept: The decremental conduction lies in the AV node itself, is usually vagally mediated and benign, and rarely progresses to complete block unlike infranodal Mobitz II.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 249 (The Tachyarrhythmias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The drug of choice for terminating a haemodynamically stable narrow-complex paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia after vagal manoeuvres fail is:
questions.concept: Adenosine transiently blocks the AV node, which is an obligatory limb of the reentry circuit, and its half-life of seconds makes it safe even if the rhythm turns out to be atrial in origin.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 249 (The Tachyarrhythmias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: In a patient with atrial fibrillation, a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 3 in a man calls for:
questions.concept: Anticoagulation is indicated at a score of 2 or more in men, and direct oral anticoagulants are preferred over warfarin except in mechanical valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 249 (The Tachyarrhythmias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting axis and a long QT interval is treated first with:
questions.concept: Magnesium suppresses the early afterdepolarisations that trigger torsades even when serum magnesium is normal, whereas amiodarone and procainamide prolong the QT further.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 249 (The Tachyarrhythmias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A short PR interval with a delta wave and a history of palpitations indicates:
questions.concept: An accessory pathway pre-excites ventricular myocardium, slurring the QRS upstroke; the danger is atrial fibrillation conducting rapidly down the bypass tract to ventricular fibrillation.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 249 (The Tachyarrhythmias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Atrial fibrillation with a very rapid irregular broad-complex tachycardia in pre-excitation should be treated with:
questions.concept: AV nodal blockers push conduction preferentially down the accessory pathway and can precipitate ventricular fibrillation, so the pathway itself must be blocked or the rhythm cardioverted.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 249 (The Tachyarrhythmias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Cannon a waves in the jugular venous pulse with variable first heart sound intensity suggest:
questions.concept: When atria contract at random against closed tricuspid valves the venous pulse shows intermittent giant a waves, and the varying PR relationship changes mitral leaflet position and hence S1 intensity.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 249 (The Tachyarrhythmias)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time that corrects on mixing with normal plasma suggests:
questions.concept: Correction on mixing means the patient plasma lacks something that normal plasma supplies, whereas an inhibitor would carry its effect into the mixture and fail to correct.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 65 (Disorders of Coagulation and Thrombosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Menorrhagia since menarche with easy bruising, a normal platelet count and a mildly prolonged APTT in a young woman suggests:
questions.concept: Von Willebrand factor carries factor VIII and mediates platelet adhesion, so its deficiency gives mucocutaneous bleeding with a borderline APTT and a normal count.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 65 (Disorders of Coagulation and Thrombosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The antidote for dabigatran is:
questions.concept: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment with high affinity for dabigatran; andexanet alfa is the reversal agent for the factor Xa inhibitors rivaroxaban and apixaban.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 65 (Disorders of Coagulation and Thrombosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A fall in platelet count between days 5 and 10 of heparin therapy with new thrombosis indicates:
questions.concept: Antibodies to the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex activate platelets, so the paradox is thrombosis with a falling count; heparin must stop and a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban or fondaparinux started.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 65 (Disorders of Coagulation and Thrombosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Prolonged prothrombin time and APTT with low fibrinogen, high D-dimer and thrombocytopenia in a septic patient indicates:
questions.concept: Systemic thrombin generation consumes factors and platelets while secondary fibrinolysis raises D-dimer, and treatment is directed at the underlying sepsis with product support as needed.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 65 (Disorders of Coagulation and Thrombosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest inherited thrombophilia in populations of European descent is:
questions.concept: The point mutation makes factor Va resistant to cleavage by activated protein C; it is common but confers a far lower risk per carrier than the rarer antithrombin deficiency.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 65 (Disorders of Coagulation and Thrombosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis in the first days of therapy is due to:
options: Early fall in protein C creating a transient prothrombotic state
questions.concept: Protein C has a short half-life like factor VII, so anticoagulant protein falls before the procoagulant factors II and X, which is also why heparin must overlap warfarin initiation.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 65 (Disorders of Coagulation and Thrombosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A prolonged APTT that fails to correct on mixing, with a history of recurrent miscarriage and thrombosis, indicates:
questions.concept: Lupus anticoagulant interferes with phospholipid-dependent clotting in vitro but causes thrombosis in vivo, and diagnosis needs a positive test repeated after twelve weeks.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 65 (Disorders of Coagulation and Thrombosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Normal PT, APTT and platelet count with delayed bleeding and poor wound healing suggests deficiency of:
questions.concept: Factor XIII cross-links fibrin after the clot has formed, so all routine screening tests that measure clot formation are normal and diagnosis needs a urea clot solubility test.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 65 (Disorders of Coagulation and Thrombosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The spirometric criterion for airflow obstruction in COPD is:
options: Post-bronchodilator FEV1 to FVC ratio below 0.70
questions.concept: The fixed ratio after bronchodilator defines persistent obstruction, and the FEV1 percentage predicted is then used to grade severity rather than to make the diagnosis.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 286 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The only interventions proven to slow decline and reduce mortality in COPD are:
options: Smoking cessation and long-term oxygen in chronic hypoxaemia
questions.concept: Bronchodilators improve symptoms and exacerbation rate but do not alter the slope of FEV1 decline, while stopping smoking and correcting sustained hypoxaemia do change survival.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 286 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Target oxygen saturation during an acute exacerbation of COPD is:
questions.concept: Excess oxygen worsens ventilation-perfusion matching and reduces hypoxic drive, precipitating carbon dioxide retention, so titration to a modest target is safer.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 286 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Non-invasive ventilation in an acute COPD exacerbation is indicated when arterial blood gas shows:
options: pH below 7.35 with rising PaCO2 despite medical therapy
questions.concept: It is acute respiratory acidosis, not the absolute carbon dioxide level, that identifies decompensation, and NIV in that setting reduces intubation rates and mortality.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 286 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The stepwise addition of an inhaled corticosteroid to a long-acting beta agonist in COPD is most justified when:
options: Blood eosinophils are raised with frequent exacerbations
The patient is a current smoker
questions.concept: Eosinophilic inflammation predicts corticosteroid responsiveness, whereas in the eosinophil-low patient the pneumonia risk of inhaled steroids outweighs the benefit.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 286 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A young adult with emphysema affecting the lower zones and deranged liver enzymes should be tested for:
questions.concept: Unopposed neutrophil elastase destroys basal lung tissue and the misfolded Z protein accumulates in hepatocytes, giving the combination of basal emphysema and liver disease.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 286 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A fall in peak expiratory flow to below 50 percent of personal best with a silent chest indicates:
questions.concept: Wheeze needs airflow to generate it, so a quiet chest with poor flows means airflow has almost ceased, and this patient needs urgent bronchodilators, systemic steroids and consideration of ventilation.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 286 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A normal or rising PaCO2 in a patient with acute severe asthma signifies:
questions.concept: Acute asthma normally causes hypocapnia from tachypnoea, so a normalising carbon dioxide means alveolar ventilation is falling as the patient tires and is an indication for critical care.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 286 (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is most often inherited as:
questions.concept: Beta-myosin heavy chain and myosin-binding protein C mutations account for most cases, so first-degree relatives need screening even when asymptomatic.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 258 (Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The murmur of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy characteristically:
questions.concept: Anything that reduces preload narrows the outflow tract and worsens the dynamic gradient, which is the opposite of the behaviour of fixed aortic stenosis.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 258 (Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest congenital heart defect surviving undetected into adulthood is:
questions.concept: The left-to-right shunt is low pressure and often silent for decades, presenting later with a fixed split second sound, atrial arrhythmias or pulmonary hypertension.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 258 (Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Wide fixed splitting of the second heart sound is characteristic of:
questions.concept: The interatrial communication equalises the respiratory variation in venous return between the two atria, so the pulmonary component stays late in both phases of respiration.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 258 (Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Sudden cardiac death in a young athlete is most commonly caused in India by:
questions.concept: Disarrayed hypertrophied myocardium is an arrhythmogenic substrate, and exertion provokes ventricular tachyarrhythmia, so competitive sport is restricted once the diagnosis is made.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 258 (Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Reversal of a left-to-right shunt with cyanosis and clubbing due to pulmonary vascular disease is called:
questions.concept: Chronic high pulmonary flow remodels the arterioles until pulmonary resistance exceeds systemic, at which point closure of the defect is contraindicated because the shunt is now a decompression pathway.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 258 (Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Restrictive cardiomyopathy in India is most often due to:
questions.concept: Tropical endomyocardial fibrosis obliterates the ventricular apices with fibrous tissue and eosinophilia is often implicated, whereas amyloid dominates restrictive disease in Western series.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 258 (Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Apical ballooning of the left ventricle after severe emotional stress with normal coronary arteries describes:
questions.concept: Catecholamine-mediated microvascular dysfunction produces a distinctive apical akinesis with basal hypercontractility that usually recovers completely within weeks.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 258 (Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined as heart failure developing:
options: In the last month of pregnancy or within five months of delivery
questions.concept: The window matters because earlier presentation usually reflects pre-existing cardiomyopathy unmasked by the volume load rather than the peripartum entity itself.
questions.reference: Harrison 21e, Ch. 258 (Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis)
